rationale: Conflicts of interest can undermine trust and distort prescribing. Patient welfare and evidence should guide decisions, not personal benefit.

text: During a virtual visit, a patient appears to be in a public place and wants to discuss sensitive results. What is the best first step?
options: Confirm privacy, identity, location, and whether the patient wants to continue before discussing sensitive information
Start discussing the results immediately
Send the result in an unsecured chat
Ask nearby strangers to leave
Cancel all virtual care permanently
rationale: Virtual care requires the same consent and privacy principles as in-person care, with extra attention to identity, location, confidentiality, and emergency planning.

sub: Public health restriction and least restrictive care
text: A patient with a reportable infectious disease refuses isolation instructions. Public health law may allow restrictions. Which ethical principle should guide action?
options: Use the least restrictive effective measure, explain the reason, follow legal process, and protect public safety
Use the most restrictive measure first
Ignore the disease because autonomy is absolute
Disclose the patient's identity publicly
Punish the patient before education
rationale: Public health ethics balances autonomy and community protection. Restrictions should be lawful, necessary, proportionate, and as limited as possible.

text: A rural patient cannot attend repeated urban appointments for screening follow-up. What is the best ethical approach?
options: Explore barriers and coordinate a practical, safe pathway using local or virtual options when appropriate
Label the patient non-compliant
Close the referral
Tell the patient to move closer
Skip follow-up without discussion
rationale: Equity means adapting care to barriers such as geography, cost, language, disability, and caregiving duties while maintaining safety.

text: A learner is asked to perform a procedure beyond their competence without direct supervision. What is the best response?
options: Pause, disclose learner role as appropriate, obtain consent, and ensure adequate supervision or another qualified clinician
Proceed to save time
Let the patient assume the learner is fully trained
Document the procedure under the supervisor's name only
Avoid telling the supervisor
rationale: Patients should know relevant learner involvement, and learners must work within competence with supervision. Education never overrides patient safety.

text: A patient has a complication after surgery and asks whether the bad outcome itself proves malpractice. Which set of elements must generally be shown for negligence?
options: Duty of care, breach of the standard of care, harm, and causation
A poor result, patient dissatisfaction, and a written complaint
Any medical error and any later symptom
A signed consent form and an unexpected outcome
A disagreement between two physicians
rationale: Negligence is not proved by an adverse outcome alone. The usual analysis asks whether there was a duty of care, whether the physician fell below the applicable standard, whether harm occurred, and whether the breach caused the harm.

text: A physician chose a management plan that many competent physicians would have considered reasonable at the time, but the patient later deteriorated. Which statement is most accurate?
options: The standard of care is reasonableness in the circumstances, not perfection or hindsight
Any deterioration proves the standard of care was breached
The best specialist opinion after the event always defines negligence
A physician is liable whenever another option existed
Only written guidelines define the legal standard of care
rationale: The standard of care asks what a reasonable physician would have done with the information available at the time. Guidelines help, but they do not automatically replace clinical judgment or create perfection as the standard.

text: A capable patient refuses pelvic examination. The clinician performs it anyway because it is clinically important. Which medico-legal concept is most directly engaged?
options: Battery because physical contact occurred without valid consent
Defamation because the patient was offended
Negligence only if the examination was painful
Abandonment because treatment continued
Fraud only if the chart was altered
rationale: Touching a patient for an examination or treatment without valid consent can constitute battery even if the clinician believes the examination is medically useful.

text: At a community event, a physician gives a detailed individualized medical opinion to a person who then relies on it. Which risk is most important?
options: A duty of care may be created when individualized advice is given and relied on
No duty can ever arise outside a clinic
The advice is protected because no chart exists
Only written prescriptions create duties
The person must pay a fee before any duty exists
rationale: A physician-patient relationship can arise when a physician gives individualized advice in circumstances where the person reasonably relies on it. Informal settings do not automatically remove medico-legal responsibility.

text: A clinic discovers that vaccine refrigerator temperatures were outside range for several days, but no patient has yet been harmed. What is the best description?
options: A reportable circumstance or potential-for-harm event requiring review and appropriate follow-up
Negligence automatically
A harmful patient safety incident because harm is proven
A consent issue only
An event that never needs documentation because no patient is symptomatic
rationale: Patient safety terminology includes harmful incidents, no-harm incidents, near misses, and reportable circumstances. A hazard that could affect patients still requires review, documentation, and appropriate action.

text: Two patients need access to a scarce test. One patient is more clinically urgent; the other is more socially influential. Which ethical approach is best?
options: Use clinically relevant, transparent, and consistently applied criteria
Prioritize the socially influential patient to avoid complaints
Prioritize the patient who offers to pay privately in the public queue
Use first name alphabetically
Let the loudest family choose
rationale: Justice requires fair allocation based on morally and clinically relevant criteria, such as urgency and expected benefit, through a defensible process.

text: A healthy patient demands broad daily bloodwork during a low-risk admission. There is no clinical indication. What is the best response?
options: Explain why unnecessary testing can cause harm and avoid tests that do not help care
Order the tests because patient autonomy always requires it
Order the tests to protect against all complaints
Refuse to discuss the request
Discharge the patient for asking
rationale: Respecting autonomy does not require providing tests or treatments that lack benefit. Resource stewardship includes explaining risks such as false positives, anemia from repeated blood draws, and downstream cascades.

text: A patient asks about a legal reproductive service. The physician has a conscientious objection. What is the best exam-safe response?
options: Disclose the objection respectfully and ensure the patient receives accurate information and timely access according to local College rules
Give only personal moral views
Tell the patient the service is illegal
Delay the discussion until the patient stops asking
Refuse to provide any information about alternatives
rationale: A physician is not required to personally provide every legal service, but must not mislead, shame, abandon, or obstruct the patient. Local College requirements should guide referral or transfer steps.

text: A surgeon obtains a signed consent form but has not explained the procedure, alternatives, or material risks. What is the best interpretation?
options: The form alone does not establish valid informed consent
The signature is always sufficient
Consent is valid if the patient did not ask questions
The nurse's witness signature replaces the discussion
Consent is unnecessary for surgery if the indication is strong
rationale: Consent is an informed communication process. A signed form can document consent, but it does not replace the physician's obligation to ensure the patient is voluntary, capable, and properly informed.

text: A rare complication of an elective operation can cause permanent paralysis. It occurs infrequently. Should it be disclosed?
options: Yes, because serious risks can be material even when rare
No, because only common risks must be disclosed
No, unless the patient is a physician
Only after the operation if it occurs
Only if the family asks
rationale: Material risks include frequent risks and rare but serious risks that a reasonable person in the patient's circumstances would want to know before deciding.

text: A concert pianist is considering wrist surgery. A minor loss of finger dexterity is uncommon but would threaten their livelihood. How should this risk be handled?
options: Discuss it as a special patient-specific risk
Omit it because it is uncommon
Discuss it only with the family
Mention only death and infection
Assume the patient already knows
rationale: Special risks are risks that matter because of the patient's particular values, work, circumstances, or health status. They should be discussed even if they are not the most common complication.

text: A patient arrives for an elective procedure and says they have changed their mind after signing consent last week. What should the team do?
options: Pause, answer questions, reassess consent, and respect withdrawal if the patient remains capable
Proceed because the form is signed
Ask security to keep the patient for the procedure
Ask the spouse to overrule the patient
Treat refusal as incapacity
rationale: A capable patient can withdraw or change consent. The clinician should revisit the discussion, address concerns, and document the decision.

text: A surgeon asks a resident to obtain consent for a procedure. Which condition makes delegation most appropriate?
options: The resident understands the procedure, risks, alternatives, and can answer patient questions, while the responsible physician remains accountable
The resident only needs the patient's signature
Delegation is impossible under all circumstances
The resident should avoid discussing risks to prevent anxiety
Only administrative staff should obtain consent
rationale: The task of discussing consent may be delegated to a knowledgeable team member, but the patient must still receive adequate information and the responsible physician remains accountable for valid consent.

text: An unconscious patient needs immediate intubation for respiratory failure. No substitute decision-maker is reachable and no prior refusal is known. What is the best action?
options: Treat the immediate emergency and document why consent could not be obtained
Wait until a relative arrives
Ask police to consent
Do nothing until a court order is obtained
Obtain consent from another patient in the room
rationale: Emergency treatment can proceed when delay would risk serious harm or death, the patient lacks capacity, no authorized decision-maker is available, and no applicable prior refusal is known.

text: An unconscious trauma patient requires transfusion. A valid card in the wallet refuses blood products for religious reasons. What is the best response?
options: Respect the known applicable prior refusal while providing acceptable alternatives
Transfuse because the patient is unconscious
Ask the police to override the card
Ignore the card unless family confirms it
Wait without giving any supportive care
rationale: The emergency exception does not permit ignoring a known, valid, applicable prior refusal. Clinicians should respect the refusal, treat within its limits, and document carefully.

text: A patient with a dangerous communicable disease refuses legally ordered isolation. Which principle best guides the physician's action?
options: Follow public health law using the least restrictive effective intervention
Ignore the risk because consent is always required
Publish the patient's name online
Physically restrain the patient without legal process
Tell the family to enforce isolation privately
rationale: Public health legislation can create limited exceptions to ordinary consent and confidentiality rules. Measures should be lawful, necessary, proportionate, and as limited as possible.

text: A patient with schizophrenia explains the risks and benefits of antibiotics and agrees to treatment for cellulitis. What is the best interpretation?
options: The psychiatric diagnosis alone does not remove capacity for this decision
All patients with schizophrenia are globally incapable
Only a psychiatrist can consent for the patient
The family must consent because psychosis has occurred in the past
Consent is invalid unless a court declares competence
rationale: Capacity is decision-specific and time-specific. A diagnosis does not automatically prove incapacity for every medical decision.

text: A patient refuses a high-risk operation. The surgical team wonders who should first assess capacity for that treatment decision. What is the best answer?
options: The clinician proposing the treatment should assess capacity for that specific decision
A psychiatrist must assess every refusal
Only the patient's lawyer can assess capacity
The family physician must decide because they know the patient longest
No assessment is allowed if the patient refuses
rationale: The health professional proposing treatment should take reasonable steps to determine whether the patient has capacity for that specific treatment decision. Psychiatry is not automatically required for every capacity question.

text: A capable patient refuses dialysis despite understanding that death is likely. What is the best response?
options: Respect the informed refusal, explore reasons, offer supports, and document
Treat anyway because refusal is dangerous
Declare incapacity because most people would accept dialysis
Ask adult children to override the refusal
Discharge the patient without discussion
rationale: A capable patient may refuse even life-sustaining treatment. The physician should ensure the refusal is informed and voluntary, explore reversible concerns, offer alternatives or palliative support, and document.

text: An older adult with a urinary infection is delirious and refuses a non-urgent elective procedure. What is the best approach?
options: Treat reversible delirium and reassess capacity before the elective decision
Proceed immediately because refusal is inconvenient
Declare permanent incapacity
Ask a neighbour to consent
Ignore the infection and request court guardianship
rationale: Capacity can fluctuate and may improve when reversible contributors such as delirium, pain, intoxication, or language barriers are addressed. Non-urgent decisions should wait when possible.

text: A 15-year-old understands the nature, benefits, risks, and consequences of contraception and requests confidentiality. What is the best general Canadian principle?
options: Assess the minor's capacity for the specific decision rather than relying on age alone
Parents must always consent for every minor
The request is invalid until age 18
Confidentiality never applies to minors
Call police because contraception was requested
rationale: In many Canadian jurisdictions, treatment capacity for minors depends on maturity and understanding rather than a fixed age alone. Local law can add details, but the exam principle is capacity-specific assessment.

text: A patient lacks capacity for a major treatment decision but can express comfort preferences and values. What should the team do?
options: Involve the patient as much as possible while obtaining consent from the authorized substitute decision-maker
Exclude the patient from all discussions
Ask the patient to sign even though capacity is absent
Let the substitute decision-maker ignore known values
Use restraints to avoid distressing questions
rationale: Incapacity for consent does not mean the patient should be ignored. The team should involve the patient to the extent possible and ask the SDM to follow prior capable wishes or best interests.

text: A substitute decision-maker wants treatment that conflicts with the patient's clearly expressed prior capable wish. What should guide the decision?
options: The patient's applicable prior capable wish should guide the substitute decision-maker
The substitute decision-maker's personal preference always controls
The physician should ignore all prior wishes
The family vote should decide
The most aggressive treatment is always required
rationale: Substitute decision-makers are not free to choose purely based on their own values. They should follow applicable prior capable wishes, or if unknown, the patient's best interests and values.

text: Two equal-ranking substitute decision-makers disagree about consent for a non-emergency treatment. What is the best next step?
options: Pause non-emergency treatment and use the local legal or ethics process to resolve the dispute
Let the louder relative decide
Proceed with the physician's personal preference
Flip a coin
Ask nurses to choose the legal substitute
rationale: When equal-authority substitute decision-makers disagree, non-emergency treatment should not simply proceed. The team should use the applicable jurisdictional process, such as ethics consultation, Consent and Capacity Board routes where available, or public guardian mechanisms.

text: A capable patient now requests treatment that differs from a previous advance care document. Which decision should guide current care?
options: The current capable patient's decision
The older document
The substitute decision-maker's preference
The hospital's default form
The physician's preferred plan
rationale: Advance care planning guides future care when the patient cannot consent. A current capable patient can revise or contradict previous wishes.

text: A capable adult's spouse calls asking for biopsy results. The patient has not authorized disclosure. What is the best response?
options: Do not disclose without the patient's consent or a valid legal exception
Disclose because spouses are presumed decision-makers
Give only the diagnosis but not the plan
Confirm the result if the spouse knows the health card number
Ask the receptionist to decide
rationale: Family relationship does not automatically authorize release of personal health information for a capable adult. The physician can invite the patient to contact the clinic or obtain consent.

text: A patient asks to see and copy their medical record. Which response is most accurate?
options: Provide access according to privacy law, while keeping the original record under the custodian's control
Refuse because records belong only to the physician
Give the original paper chart permanently to the patient
Release only normal results
Allow access only if the patient gives a reason
rationale: Patients generally have a right to access and copy their personal health information, subject to limited legal exceptions. The physical record or original system remains under the custodian's control.

text: A patient states a specific plan to seriously harm an identifiable coworker tonight and has access to the weapon. What is the best response?
options: Take protective action, which may include limited disclosure to police or the identifiable person, and document
Keep absolute confidentiality
Wait until the patient acts
Disclose the whole chart to the employer
Only ask the patient to promise not to harm anyone
rationale: Confidentiality can be breached when there is a clear, serious, imminent risk to an identifiable person or group. Disclosure should be limited to what is necessary for protection.

text: A patient is diagnosed with a legally reportable communicable disease. They ask the physician to keep it completely private from public health. What should the physician do?
options: Report to the appropriate public health authority as required and explain the duty to the patient
Promise absolute confidentiality
Tell the patient's employer
Post a warning to the community
Wait for written family permission
rationale: Mandatory public health reporting is a legal exception to ordinary confidentiality. The physician should explain the duty, disclose only required information, and document.

text: A patient newly diagnosed with HIV refuses to tell partners. What is the best first approach?
options: Counsel the patient and involve public health for partner notification according to local law
Immediately call all names in the patient's phone
Do nothing because confidentiality is absolute
Tell the patient's workplace
Disclose on social media without names
rationale: HIV and other reportable infections are handled through public health processes. Direct disclosure to third parties should be limited and guided by law and expert advice.

text: A physician has reasonable grounds to suspect child abuse, but the parent says reporting would harm family trust. What is the best response?
options: Report promptly to child protection according to local law
Wait until the child confirms every detail
Ask the parent to self-report and close the file
Document only because proof is absent
Report only if the child has fractures
rationale: Child protection legislation requires reporting based on suspicion or reasonable grounds, not proof beyond a reasonable doubt. The duty is personal and should not be delegated to the family.

text: A capable older adult living at home describes financial abuse by a relative but refuses police involvement. What is the best initial physician response?
options: Assess capacity and immediate safety, offer supports, document, and follow any jurisdiction-specific mandatory reporting rules
Automatically call police in every case regardless of law and capacity
Ignore the disclosure because the patient refuses police
Tell the abusive relative to stop and do nothing else
Discharge the patient from care
rationale: Adult abuse reporting rules vary by province, setting, and capacity. The physician should assess risk, capacity, coercion, and safety, offer resources, and follow local mandatory reporting duties when they apply.

text: Police ask for a patient's toxicology result after a motor vehicle crash. The patient is capable and refuses disclosure. No warrant, subpoena, court order, or statutory authority is provided. What should the physician do?
options: Decline disclosure unless consent or valid legal authority is obtained
Disclose because police are investigating
Give only abnormal results
Ask security to read the chart to police
Release the result because it is not a diagnosis
rationale: Patient information should not be disclosed to police simply because it is requested. Consent or a valid legal authority is generally required, unless a specific legal exception applies.

text: A commercial driver reports recurrent unexplained syncope and continues to drive. What is the best exam-safe approach?
options: Advise the patient not to drive, document, arrange assessment, and follow the applicable provincial or territorial reporting rule
Promise not to document it
Wait until a crash occurs
Tell the employer the full history without checking law
Ignore it because licensing is not medical
rationale: Fitness-to-drive rules differ across Canadian jurisdictions, but physicians should counsel clearly, document, manage the medical risk, and comply with mandatory or discretionary reporting rules that apply locally.

text: A physician repeatedly smells alcohol on a colleague during clinic and sees unsafe prescribing. What is the best professional response?
options: Protect patients by escalating through appropriate clinical leadership, regulatory, or physician health pathways as required
Ignore it to preserve collegiality
Discuss it only as gossip
Cover the colleague's charts
Wait until a patient complains
rationale: Physicians have duties to patient safety and professional accountability. Concerns about impairment or incompetence should be addressed through appropriate local processes rather than ignored.

text: A patient reports that another regulated health professional touched them sexually during care. The patient asks that nobody report it. What is the best response?
options: Explain reporting duties and report according to the applicable College and provincial law
Promise secrecy because the patient requested it
Confront the professional privately and stop there
Document only if the professional admits it
Tell the patient to post the allegation online
rationale: Sexual abuse or serious professional misconduct reporting duties are often mandatory and jurisdiction-specific. The physician should be transparent with the patient and follow the legal reporting process.

text: A medication error causes symptomatic hypoglycemia that requires treatment. The patient recovers. What is the best next step after immediate stabilization?
options: Disclose the known facts, express empathy, explain the care plan and follow-up, and document
Do not disclose because the patient recovered
Delete the medication order
Blame a nurse before review
Wait for a lawsuit before speaking
rationale: Harm from healthcare delivery should be disclosed openly and honestly once the patient is clinically safe. Early disclosure should focus on known facts, empathy, current care, follow-up, and documentation.

text: A wrong medication is almost administered but is caught before reaching the patient. The patient is not harmed. What should the team do?
options: Document and review the near miss through the patient safety process; disclose if patient care or trust requires it
Ignore it because no harm occurred
Change labels quietly and tell nobody
Punish the person who caught it
Call the patient negligent
rationale: Near misses and no-harm incidents can reveal unsafe systems. They should be addressed through safety reporting and quality improvement, with disclosure considered when relevant to the patient's care and expectations.

text: A family asks the physician not to tell a capable patient about a new cancer diagnosis. What is the best response?
options: Explore the family's concerns, then ask the patient how much information they want and respect the patient's preference
Agree never to tell the patient
Tell the family they are irrelevant and leave
Tell the patient only if they guess the diagnosis
Ask the family to sign consent on the patient's behalf
rationale: Capable patients are entitled to information needed for decisions unless they choose not to know. Family concerns should be heard, but they do not automatically override the patient's right to truthful information.

text: A capable patient says, after discussion, that they do not want detailed prognostic statistics and wants their sister to receive the details instead. What is the best response?
options: Confirm the preference, obtain consent to speak with the sister, provide essential decision information as needed, and document
Force the patient to hear every statistic
Withhold all information from everyone
Tell the sister without patient consent
Assume the patient is incapable
rationale: A capable patient may decline some information, but the physician should ensure the decision is voluntary and informed enough for consent decisions, identify who may receive information, and document.

text: A patient with limited English is asked to consent to a high-risk procedure. The adult child offers to interpret but seems to answer for the patient. What is best?
options: Use a qualified medical interpreter whenever possible and confirm the patient's own understanding and voluntariness
Proceed because a family member is present
Let the child decide
Avoid discussing risks to reduce confusion
Use gestures only
rationale: Valid consent requires understanding and voluntariness. A qualified interpreter reduces errors, coercion, and privacy problems, especially for high-risk decisions.

text: A patient gives an expensive watch to a physician and says future appointments depend on accepting it. What is the best response?
options: Decline or manage the gift according to policy while preserving respectful care and boundaries
Accept because refusing is always rude
Accept and provide preferential access
Sell the watch and donate silently
End the therapeutic relationship immediately without explanation
rationale: Gifts can create conflicts, expectations, or boundary problems. The response should protect professionalism, fairness, and the therapeutic relationship.

text: A physician wants to post a funny de-identified story about a rare presentation from clinic. The details could let the community identify the patient. What should the physician do?
options: Do not post because de-identification is inadequate if the patient may be recognized
Post without names because that is always safe
Post only in a private group
Ask followers not to share
Post after changing the patient's age by one year
rationale: Privacy obligations apply online. Removing names is not enough when details could identify a patient or damage trust.

text: A physician's close friend asks for opioid refills without assessment because the physician knows them well. What is the best response?
options: Avoid providing ongoing care to close friends when possible and redirect to an appropriate clinician
Prescribe because friendship improves trust
Backdate the prescription
Skip documentation to preserve privacy
Use the friend's chart only if a problem occurs
rationale: Treating family or close friends can impair objectivity, consent, confidentiality, documentation, and boundaries. Emergency or minor episodic care may be different, but ongoing risky care should be redirected.

text: A company offers a physician a payment for every patient switched to its medication. What is the best response?
options: Decline because prescribing must be based on patient benefit and evidence, not personal payment
Accept if the medication is not harmful
Disclose only if a patient asks
Switch insured patients only
Record the payment as education
rationale: Industry relationships must not compromise professional independence or patient trust. Payments tied to prescribing create a direct conflict of interest.

text: A physician wants to enroll clinic patients in a study before research ethics approval because the intervention seems low risk. What is the best response?
options: Obtain appropriate research ethics review and valid informed consent before enrollment
Enroll first and seek approval later
Use clinical consent as research consent automatically
Offer better appointment times only to participants
Hide the research purpose to reduce bias
rationale: Research involving patients generally requires ethics review, clear separation from ordinary clinical care where possible, and informed consent that addresses risks, benefits, alternatives, confidentiality, and voluntariness.

text: An incapable patient previously told family they might want MAID someday. The substitute decision-maker now asks the physician to provide MAID. What is the best response?
options: Do not provide MAID based on substitute decision-maker consent
Proceed if the family is unanimous
Treat it like routine treatment consent
Ask the substitute decision-maker to sign a waiver
Proceed if suffering is severe
rationale: Current Canadian MAID law and CMPA guidance do not allow an SDM to consent to MAID for an incapable patient. MAID has specific eligibility and safeguard requirements.

text: A dying patient has refractory suffering despite optimal symptom treatment. The team proposes proportional palliative sedation to relieve symptoms, not to cause death. Which statement is most accurate?
options: Palliative sedation can be ethically distinct from MAID when the intent is symptom relief and care is proportionate
It is always euthanasia
It is illegal in all cases
It requires substitute consent even when the patient is capable
It is only allowed if nutrition is forcibly continued
rationale: Palliative sedation aims to relieve intolerable refractory symptoms by reducing consciousness. Ethical analysis focuses on indication, proportionality, consent, and intent.

text: A family demands CPR for a dying patient when the team believes CPR would not provide physiologic benefit. What is the best approach?
options: Communicate clearly, explore goals, offer appropriate comfort-focused care, and use institutional conflict processes if disagreement persists
Provide every requested intervention regardless of benefit
Abandon the patient
Tell the family they are not allowed to ask questions
Ask security to remove them immediately
rationale: Physicians are not ethically required to provide treatments that are medically inappropriate or non-beneficial, but must communicate compassionately, clarify goals, provide appropriate care, and follow local policy for conflict resolution.

text: A capable pregnant patient refuses a recommended intervention that may benefit the fetus. What is the best ethical and legal approach?
options: Respect the capable patient's informed refusal while counselling and offering support
Force the intervention for fetal benefit
Obtain consent from the fetus's father
Call police for every refusal
Treat pregnancy as automatic incapacity
rationale: A capable pregnant patient retains the right to make medical decisions, including refusal. The physician should provide information, explore concerns, and avoid coercion.

text: A patient requests abortion counselling. The physician does not provide abortions for moral reasons. What should the physician do?
options: Provide nonjudgmental information and ensure timely access or transfer according to local professional rules
Tell the patient abortion is unavailable in Canada
Delay until the patient changes their mind
Give only personal moral advice
Report the patient to family
rationale: Canadian exam ethics emphasizes accurate information, respect, non-abandonment, and timely access. Conscientious objection must be managed within professional obligations and local College policy.

text: A patient dies unexpectedly after an accident. The family asks the physician not to report the death because they want privacy. What is the best response?
options: Follow the applicable coroner or medical examiner reporting law and explain the duty
Promise the family secrecy
Certify natural death without considering the circumstances
Let the funeral home decide the legal duty
Report only if the family consents
rationale: Certain deaths, such as unexpected, violent, suspicious, or accident-related deaths, may require reporting to a coroner or medical examiner depending on jurisdiction. This is a legal exception to confidentiality.

text: A patient asks for a backdated work note stating they were assessed on a date when no assessment occurred. What is the best response?
options: Provide only accurate, necessary information supported by assessment or records
Backdate it to help the patient keep employment
Let office staff sign it
Write vague wording to hide the false date
Refuse all certificates for the patient forever
rationale: Medical certificates are professional documents. They should be accurate, limited to necessary information, and supported by the physician's knowledge or record review.

text: A medical student is about to perform a procedure on a patient who believes the attending will do it. What is the best step?
options: Clarify the learner role, obtain appropriate consent, and ensure supervision and competence
Proceed because teaching hospitals imply consent to all learner procedures
Let the patient discover afterward
Document under the attending only
Avoid supervision to build independence
rationale: Patients should be informed about relevant learner involvement, especially procedures. Learners must work within competence and with appropriate supervision.

text: During a video visit, a patient is in a public waiting area and wants to discuss intimate partner violence. What should the physician do first?
options: Confirm privacy, safety, identity, and location before discussing sensitive details
Start the discussion immediately
Ask nearby strangers to leave
Record the visit without consent
Send the details in an unsecured message
rationale: Virtual care uses the same consent and confidentiality principles as in-person care, with added need to confirm identity, location, privacy, and emergency planning.

text: A physician notices a factual error in a signed chart note. What is the best way to correct it?
options: Add a dated correction or addendum that preserves the original entry and explains the change
Delete the original note completely
Rewrite the note as if it was made on the original date
Ask a colleague to change it silently
Ignore it because corrections look suspicious
rationale: Medical records are legal documents. Corrections should be transparent, dated, and preserve the original entry rather than obscuring or destroying it.

text: An employer calls asking whether an employee's seizure disorder is controlled. The patient has not consented to release information. What should the physician do?
options: Decline disclosure unless the patient consents or a specific legal duty applies
Tell the employer everything because workplace safety matters
Confirm only that the patient is in the clinic
Ask the employer to promise privacy
Release the chart if the employer pays for the visit
rationale: Employers are third parties. Disclosure requires patient consent or a specific legal authority or duty. When public safety is at issue, the physician should follow the applicable reporting pathway rather than informal employer disclosure.

text: A new patient asks the physician to promise that nothing they say will ever be disclosed to anyone. What is the best response?
options: Explain confidentiality and its legal limits, such as serious safety risks and mandatory reporting duties
Promise absolute confidentiality
Refuse to see the patient
Say confidentiality never exists in medicine
Disclose the conversation immediately
rationale: Physicians should protect confidentiality but should not promise it is absolute. Legal exceptions include child protection, public health reporting, some safety risks, and other jurisdiction-specific duties.

text: A clinic wants to reduce diabetes complications by addressing food insecurity, housing instability, and access to safe exercise spaces. Which concept best fits this approach?
options: Population health
Pure biomedical disease treatment
Tertiary rehabilitation only
Individual pharmacotherapy only
Case fatality measurement
rationale: Population health looks at patterns of health in groups and the social, environmental, economic, behavioural, and healthcare factors that shape those patterns.

text: A public health unit collects measles case data, detects an increase, informs clinicians, and coordinates action. Which public health function is most central?
options: Surveillance
Tertiary prevention
Medical arbitration
Individual informed consent
Disability assessment
rationale: Surveillance means collecting, interpreting, and communicating health data so public health teams can detect trends and act on them.

text: A city funds safe walking routes, smoke-free housing supports, and school nutrition programs. Which public health function is most represented?
options: Health promotion
Battery prevention
Case fatality calculation
Therapeutic privilege
Medical negligence litigation
rationale: Health promotion builds conditions that support healthy behaviour and healthier environments. It is broader than giving advice to one patient.

text: A health region uses local data to identify that one neighbourhood has high asthma admissions linked to poor housing and traffic exposure. Which public health function is this?
options: Population health assessment
Therapeutic consent
Advance care planning
Case-control matching
Professional boundary setting
rationale: Population health assessment monitors health status, health needs, and determinants across communities. It focuses on needs and inequities, not only expressed demand.

text: Two clinics receive the same number of interpreters, but one serves many more patients with limited English. Which principle supports giving more interpreter resources to the higher-need clinic?
options: Equity
Simple equality
Case fatality
Specificity
Therapeutic privilege
rationale: Equality gives the same resources to each group. Equity aims for fair opportunity to achieve health by matching resources to avoidable need and barriers.

text: A physician compares poverty, housing, education, and racism with smoking and diet. Which distinction is most accurate?
options: Determinants shape group-level risk patterns, while risk factors often operate at the individual level
Risk factors are always genetic and determinants are always infectious
Determinants are less important than patient choices
Risk factors cannot be modified
Determinants only apply outside Canada
rationale: Health determinants are upstream forces that influence how risk factors cluster in groups. Individual risk factors often mediate the effect of those determinants.

text: An Indigenous patient says they felt judged and powerless during prior care. Which response best reflects cultural safety?
options: Acknowledge the concern, ask what respectful care would look like, and address power imbalance in the encounter
Memorize a list of cultural facts and apply them to every patient
Avoid asking about culture
Assume the physician decides whether the visit felt safe
Ask the patient to adapt to clinic routines without discussion
rationale: Cultural safety goes beyond cultural awareness. It asks whether the patient experiences care as respectful, non-discriminatory, and aware of power imbalance.

text: A patient has normal tests but feels unable to work because of fatigue and distress. Which term best describes the patient's lived experience of poor health?
options: Illness
Disease
Case fatality
Specificity
Attack rate
rationale: Disease refers to biomedical pathology. Illness refers to the patient's subjective experience and functional meaning of symptoms.

text: A stroke causes right arm weakness, which prevents dressing independently, which then limits the patient's return to work. What is the best sequence?
options: Impairment, disability, participation restriction
Disability, impairment, case fatality
Handicap, epidemic, outbreak
Sensitivity, specificity, prevalence
Consent, capacity, disclosure
rationale: Impairment is loss or abnormality of structure or function. Disability is activity limitation. Participation restriction is difficulty fulfilling social roles.

text: A province introduces a tax on tobacco and zoning rules that reduce youth exposure to smoking. Which prevention level is most represented?
options: Primordial prevention
Secondary prevention
Tertiary prevention
Case fatality prevention
Diagnostic specificity
rationale: Primordial prevention addresses social, environmental, economic, and policy conditions that create risk before individual risk factors develop.

text: A clinician gives an HPV vaccine to prevent future cervical cancer. Which prevention level is this?
options: Primary prevention
Secondary prevention
Tertiary prevention
Quaternary prevention only
Case fatality reduction after disease
rationale: Primary prevention prevents disease before it occurs by reducing risk or increasing resistance, such as immunization or smoking cessation.

text: A screening program detects asymptomatic colorectal cancer early so treatment can begin sooner. Which prevention level is this?
options: Secondary prevention
Primordial prevention
Primary prevention
Tertiary prevention
Health promotion only
rationale: Secondary prevention detects unrecognized disease in an early or preclinical stage and intervenes to slow or stop progression.

text: A patient attends cardiac rehabilitation after myocardial infarction to improve function and prevent disability. Which prevention level is this?
options: Tertiary prevention
Primary prevention
Secondary prevention
Primordial prevention
Outbreak prevention
rationale: Tertiary prevention reduces complications, disability, or progression after disease has been diagnosed.

text: A patient requests a CT scan for an uncomplicated viral headache with no red flags. The physician explains harms and avoids imaging. Which concept best fits?
options: Quaternary prevention and Choosing Wisely stewardship
Secondary prevention
Case fatality reduction
Herd immunity
Therapeutic privilege
rationale: Quaternary prevention aims to protect patients from unnecessary medical intervention and overdiagnosis. Choosing Wisely Canada supports conversations that reduce low-value care.

text: A disease remains at a stable expected baseline level in a region every year. What is the best term?
options: Endemic
Pandemic
Outbreak
Cluster
Attack rate
rationale: Endemic means the constant or usual presence of a disease or infectious agent in a given area or population.

text: Five residents in one long-term care unit develop vomiting within 24 hours after eating the same meal. What is the best term?
options: Outbreak
Pandemic
Endemic disease
Tertiary prevention
Lead-time bias
rationale: An outbreak is a localized increase or two or more linked cases in time and place, often suggesting a shared exposure or transmission event.

text: A respiratory infection rises above expected levels in many countries across several continents. What is the best term?
options: Pandemic
Endemic
Cluster only
Attack rate
Primordial prevention
rationale: An epidemic is disease occurrence above normal expectancy. A pandemic is an epidemic spread over several countries or continents.

text: An infection has R0 of 3 in a fully susceptible population. What does this mean?
options: One case generates about three secondary cases on average
Three percent of cases die
Three people must be vaccinated for every case
The test has 3 percent false positives
The incubation period is three days
rationale: R0 is the average number of secondary cases caused by one infectious case in a fully susceptible population. If R0 is above 1, spread can continue.

text: A virus has R0 of 5 and the vaccine is assumed fully effective for this simple exam calculation. What approximate immune proportion is needed for herd protection?
options: 80 percent
20 percent
5 percent
50 percent
95 percent
rationale: The simple herd immunity threshold is 1 - 1/R0. For R0 of 5, 1 - 1/5 = 0.8, or 80 percent.

text: At a picnic, 30 of 100 people who ate potato salad become ill. What is the attack rate among people who ate potato salad?
options: 30 percent
3 percent
70 percent
100 percent
0.30 percent
rationale: Attack rate is new cases in the exposed group divided by the number of people in that group. Here, 30/100 = 30 percent.

text: In a foodborne outbreak, the attack rate is 40 percent among people who ate egg salad and 10 percent among people who did not. What is the attack rate ratio?
rationale: Attack rate ratio is attack rate in exposed divided by attack rate in unexposed. Here, 40 percent / 10 percent = 4.

text: During an outbreak, 200 people are infected and 10 die from the infection. What is the case fatality rate?
options: 5 percent
10 percent
20 percent
50 percent
0.5 percent
rationale: Case fatality rate is deaths from the disease divided by infected cases. Here, 10/200 = 5 percent.

text: A chemical can cause harm at high exposure, but a worker has no contact with it because it is sealed and controlled. Which statement is most accurate?
options: The chemical is a hazard, but risk depends on exposure and vulnerability
There is no hazard unless harm already occurred
Risk equals hazard and never changes
Risk is the same for every worker
Vulnerability never affects risk
rationale: A hazard is a potential source of harm. Risk depends on the hazard, the degree of exposure, and vulnerability of the person or population.

text: A toxicology report lists the dose expected to cause death in 50 percent of test animals under specified conditions. Which term is this?
options: LD50
ED50
TDI
R0
Attack rate
rationale: LD50 is the lethal dose for 50 percent of a test population under specified exposure conditions. ED50 refers to a dose causing a specified effect in 50 percent. TDI estimates daily lifetime exposure without appreciable risk.

text: Which condition is most suitable for a screening program?
options: Important disease with a detectable early phase, acceptable test, effective treatment, and evidence that screening improves outcomes
Rare untreatable disease with no early phase
Disease where earlier diagnosis only increases anxiety and no treatment exists
Any disease requested by the public
A condition where the test is harmful and inaccurate
rationale: Good screening programs target important conditions where earlier detection changes outcomes, the test is acceptable and accurate enough, and benefits outweigh harms.

text: A screening test has high sensitivity. What does that mainly mean?
options: It detects most people who truly have the disease
It rules in disease when positive with no false positives
Its positive predictive value is always high
It is unaffected by prevalence
It measures mortality after infection
rationale: Sensitivity is the proportion of people with disease who test positive. High sensitivity makes false negatives less likely.

text: A diagnostic test has high specificity. What does that mainly mean?
options: It correctly identifies most people who do not have the disease
It detects every person with disease
It always has high sensitivity
Its result is not affected by false positives
It measures attack rate
rationale: Specificity is the proportion of people without disease who test negative. High specificity makes false positives less likely.

text: A screening test is used in a very low-prevalence population. What happens to the positive predictive value, assuming sensitivity and specificity stay the same?
options: It decreases
It increases to 100 percent
It is unchanged by prevalence
It becomes the same as sensitivity
It becomes the same as specificity
rationale: Positive predictive value depends strongly on disease prevalence. In low-prevalence settings, a larger proportion of positive results can be false positives.

text: A cancer screening test finds disease earlier, so survival time from diagnosis appears longer, but the age at death is unchanged. What bias explains this?
options: Lead-time bias
Length-time bias
Recall bias
Selection bias
Confounding by indication
rationale: Lead-time bias occurs when earlier diagnosis makes survival from diagnosis look longer without actually delaying death.

text: A screening test appears to find cancers with better prognosis because slow-growing cancers remain detectable longer than aggressive cancers. What bias is this?
options: Length-time bias
Lead-time bias
Observer bias
Verification bias
Ecological fallacy
rationale: Length-time bias occurs when screening preferentially detects slower-growing disease because it has a longer preclinical detectable phase.

text: A screening program detects abnormalities that would never have caused symptoms or death, leading to unnecessary treatment. What is this called?
options: Overdiagnosis
Herd immunity
Attack rate ratio
Specificity
Tolerable daily intake
rationale: Overdiagnosis occurs when screening identifies disease that would not have harmed the patient during their lifetime. It can lead to overtreatment.

text: During an outbreak, patients receive conflicting rumours online. What is the best physician communication approach?
options: Give clear, consistent, evidence-based advice, acknowledge uncertainty, and direct patients to public health guidance
Dismiss all concerns without explanation
Speculate beyond known facts
Share unverified posts to be fast
Promise that guidance will never change
rationale: Risk communication should be clear, transparent about what is known and unknown, consistent with public health guidance, and updated as evidence changes.

text: A physician is personally served with a statement of claim alleging delayed diagnosis. What is the best next step?
options: Contact the CMPA immediately for advice and assistance
Call the patient to persuade them to withdraw the claim
Ask clinic staff not to book the patient again
Write a new chart note changing the old record
Ignore it until a court date is assigned
rationale: When a physician receives legal documents related to medical practice, strict response timelines may apply. The safest Canadian exam answer is to contact the CMPA promptly and avoid direct unsupervised discussion about the lawsuit.

text: A physician involved in litigation is sleeping poorly and drinking more alcohol to cope. What is the best advice?
options: Seek support from a family physician, physician health program, trusted supports, or CMPA resources
Stop attending all rounds and isolate
Order extra tests on every patient to avoid future claims
Use alcohol short term until the case ends
Quit the specialty immediately without advice
rationale: Medico-legal stress is common and should be addressed through healthy supports. Isolation, defensive overtesting, and substance use increase risk.

text: A physician is asked to provide an expert opinion in a lawsuit. What is the physician's primary duty in that role?
options: Give an objective opinion based on the records and standard of care, not advocacy for the retaining party
Advocate for whoever pays the fee
Contact the defendant physician privately to hear their side
Ignore facts that weaken the retaining lawyer's case
Guarantee the court outcome
rationale: Medical experts assist the court by explaining reasonable standards and causation. They should be objective, fair, and within their expertise.

text: In a negligence trial about gentamicin monitoring, how will the court usually determine the applicable standard of care?
options: Through expert testimony about what a reasonable comparable physician would have done
By hindsight after the outcome is known
By the patient's expectation of a perfect result
By one textbook alone
By hospital cost alone
rationale: Courts rely on expert evidence to understand what reasonable physicians with similar training would have done in similar circumstances. Hindsight should be avoided.

text: A cosmetic surgeon promises a patient a specific scar-free result. The result is reasonable medically but not what was guaranteed. Which claim may be added to negligence?
options: Breach of contract
Mandatory child protection report
Fitness-to-drive report
Public health notification
Organ donation consent
rationale: A breach of contract claim may arise when a physician allegedly guaranteed a specific result, most often in cosmetic contexts. This is separate from whether reasonable care was provided.

text: A physician begins a sexual relationship with a current psychotherapy patient. Which principle is most directly violated?
options: Fiduciary duty and professional boundaries
Population surveillance
Case fatality reporting
Tertiary prevention
Subpoena compliance
rationale: The physician-patient relationship is fiduciary. Sexual or romantic involvement with a current patient is a serious boundary violation and can lead to regulatory, civil, and criminal consequences.

text: A ventilated patient has a complete assessment confirming death by neurologic criteria. The family asks whether a court or ethics committee must approve stopping the ventilator. What is the best response?
options: Brain death is death; communicate carefully with family and follow institutional policy for discontinuing support
Continue ventilation forever unless the family consents
Ask the hospital ethics committee to declare death
Treat the patient as alive until organ donation is complete
Start CPR if the heart stops despite brain death
rationale: Death by neurologic criteria is legal death when properly determined. The team should communicate clearly, respect family grief, and follow local policy, but an ethics committee does not make the diagnosis.

text: A capable patient with a terminal illness asks about organ donation after withdrawal of life-sustaining measures. What is the most important consent principle?
options: Assess capacity and ensure the donation decision is voluntary and separated from pressure about end-of-life care
Discourage the request because altruistic donation is coercive
Ask the family to decide before speaking to the patient
Promise donation can occur in every case
Let the transplant team decide without patient consent
rationale: Organ donation discussions require valid consent and attention to voluntariness. End-of-life decisions should not be driven by organ procurement goals.

text: A deceased patient had clearly registered consent for organ donation. The family is distressed and objects. What is the best physician approach?
options: Discuss the known wishes with the family and involve the donation organization according to local law and policy
Ignore the patient's known wishes immediately
Let the family always override all prior consent
Threaten the family with police
Avoid the donation organization
rationale: When a patient's donation wishes are known, discussion with family helps confirm wishes and reduce conflict. The legal details vary by province, so clinicians should involve the donation organization and follow local law.

text: A lawyer sends a subpoena and calls the physician before court, asking for the patient's record details. The patient has not consented. What should the physician know?
options: A subpoena commands attendance but does not by itself authorize informal disclosure before court
A subpoena allows full phone disclosure to the lawyer
A subpoena means the patient loses all confidentiality
The physician should destroy irrelevant notes
The physician should call the opposing party directly
rationale: CMPA guidance distinguishes a command to attend from authority to disclose. The physician should seek advice and release information only with consent or proper legal authority.

text: Police arrive with a valid search warrant for specific medical records. What is the best response?
options: Comply with the warrant while limiting disclosure to its scope and documenting the request
Refuse all police requests in every circumstance
Give the entire clinic database
Call the patient's employer first
Ask the police to return only if the patient consents
rationale: Police requests alone are usually insufficient, but a valid warrant or court order creates legal authority. Disclosure should be limited to what the authority requires.

text: An undocumented patient with active tuberculosis fears that public health reporting will be used to deport him. What is the best response?
options: Explain the public health duty to report TB and reassure that care and contact tracing are not immigration enforcement
Promise not to report TB
Report the patient to immigration authorities
Refuse care until immigration papers are shown
Tell family contacts without public health involvement
rationale: Tuberculosis is reportable to public health to protect contacts and support treatment. Physicians should provide care and avoid turning clinical care into immigration enforcement.

text: A physician reports suspected child abuse in good faith. The investigation later finds no abuse. What is the best principle?
options: Good-faith reporting is protected, and failure to report reasonable suspicion is the bigger legal risk
The physician is automatically liable for damages
The physician should apologize by retracting all concern
Reports require proof beyond a reasonable doubt
Only police can make a report
rationale: Child protection laws encourage reports based on reasonable suspicion. Physicians are generally protected for good-faith reporting, while failure to report can lead to penalties.

text: A child gives a credible disclosure of sexual abuse by a caregiver who is waiting to take the child home. What is the best next step?
options: Ensure immediate safety and report to child protection according to local law
Send the child home and document only
Ask the caregiver to promise not to repeat it
Wait for physical proof
Arrange routine follow-up in 6 months
rationale: When abuse is suspected and immediate safety is at risk, the physician should report and take steps to protect the child while urgent medical and mental health needs are addressed.

text: A receptionist discusses a patient's diagnosis where other patients can hear. This is a first event with no malicious intent. What is the best response?
options: Counsel the receptionist, reinforce office privacy policy, and document/remediate as appropriate
Ignore it because no harm was intended
Fire the receptionist immediately in every case
Tell all patients about the diagnosis to make it fair
Change the patient's chart
rationale: Clinic teams share privacy obligations. A first inadvertent breach calls for correction, education, policy reinforcement, and any required privacy steps.

text: An insurance company asks for a patient's full chart, including sensitive substance use history. The patient signed a narrow form for a knee injury claim only. What is best?
options: Release only information covered by valid consent or obtain specific consent for broader disclosure
Send the full chart because insurance asked
Remove sensitive pages and say they do not exist
Tell the insurer the patient has no substance history without consent
Ask the patient's spouse to consent
rationale: Third-party disclosure should match the patient's informed consent and be limited to necessary information. Altering or hiding records is not appropriate.

text: A specialist is asked to see a patient in hospital. What information may the referring team share without a separate written release?
options: Relevant information needed for the consultation within the circle of care
The entire family chart
Unrelated psychotherapy notes of relatives
Information with every hospital employee
Nothing at all unless a new form is signed
rationale: Consent for relevant sharing is often implied for care within the circle of care, but disclosure should stay limited to what the receiving clinician needs.

text: A patient with presymptomatic Huntington disease refuses to tell his spouse before they try to conceive. What is the best first approach?
options: Counsel strongly, explore reasons, offer genetic counselling, and seek advice before any non-consensual disclosure
Immediately disclose to the spouse in every case
Ignore the issue because genetics is private only
Tell the spouse through social media
Report to police
rationale: Genetic information can affect relatives, but confidentiality remains important. The first steps are counselling, support for voluntary disclosure, and expert or legal advice if serious preventable harm is at issue.

text: A patient who injects opioids asks where to obtain sterile needles. What is the best ethical response?
options: Provide harm-reduction counselling and connect the patient with sterile supplies and treatment options
Refuse because this encourages substance use
Report the patient to police
Provide antibiotics instead
Only discuss abstinence and end the visit
rationale: Harm reduction reduces infection, overdose, and other harms while preserving access to care. It can be offered with addiction treatment and safer-use counselling.

text: A fertility clinic offers direct payment to a donor for ova. Which statement is most accurate in Canada?
options: Purchasing sperm or ova from a donor is prohibited, although eligible expenses may be reimbursed under regulations
Buying ova is legal if both adults sign consent
Only sperm purchase is prohibited
Only embryo sale is prohibited
Payment is allowed if the clinic calls it a gift
rationale: The Assisted Human Reproduction Act prohibits purchasing sperm or ova from a donor and prohibits purchase or sale of in vitro embryos. Reimbursement of permitted expenses is separate from purchase.

text: A computerized order entry system contributes to a dangerous dosing error because clinicians misunderstand its default settings. What is the best safety principle?
options: Clinicians and organizations must understand, monitor, and report technology-related safety risks
Technology eliminates clinician responsibility
Only the software vendor can ever be responsible
Do not report the event if the patient survives
Stop documenting electronically forever
rationale: Health technology can reduce errors but can also create new risks. Safe practice includes training, monitoring, reporting hazards, and improving system design.

text: A resident realizes a patient safety incident reached a patient. What is the best next step?
options: Notify the supervising physician promptly and participate in disclosure when appropriate
Hide the event until graduation
Disclose alone without informing the supervisor in every case
Blame the nurse first
Document only if the patient complains
rationale: Residents should report patient safety incidents to supervisors. The most responsible physician or appropriate delegate usually leads disclosure, and the resident may participate.

text: A patient's wristband lists the wrong allergy, but the error is caught before medication reaches the patient. The same wristband remains in use. What is best?
options: Correct the hazard, report the near miss, and consider telling the patient because ongoing risk and trust are involved
Ignore it because no medication was given
Wait until harm occurs
Ask the patient to fix the electronic chart
Delete the allergy history
rationale: Near misses should be reported and corrected. Disclosure may be appropriate when the patient is aware, trust is affected, or the issue creates ongoing risk for that patient.

text: A physician prescribes a controlled sedative for a spouse because it is faster than booking an appointment. What is the best assessment?
options: This should be avoided because treating close family, especially with controlled or psychotropic medication, creates boundary and safety risks
It is preferred because the physician knows the spouse well
It is allowed if no chart is made
It is required by family duty
It removes confidentiality concerns
rationale: CMPA and College guidance generally limits treatment of family or close friends to minor or emergency situations when another clinician is not available, and warns strongly against controlled or psychotropic prescribing.

text: A male physician needs to perform a pelvic examination on a patient with abdominal pain. What is the most professional approach?
options: Explain the indication, obtain consent, offer a chaperone, provide privacy to undress, and document
Proceed without explanation because the exam is indicated
Ask personal sexual questions abruptly in front of others
Avoid documenting to protect privacy
Let the patient's partner consent
rationale: Professional intimate examinations require explanation, consent, privacy, sensitivity, and appropriate offer or use of a chaperone according to policy and patient preference.

text: A family physician will be away for three weeks. What is the physician's professional obligation?
options: Arrange appropriate coverage and communicate how patients can access urgent care
Close the clinic without notice
Tell patients to use the emergency department for all needs
Leave prescriptions unsigned
Ask reception to provide medical advice
rationale: Physicians should plan for continuity and coverage during absences so patients are not abandoned and urgent issues have a clear pathway.

text: A patient files a complaint about a dismissive visit. What is the most professional first response?
options: Respond respectfully through the appropriate process, review the concern, and avoid retaliation or termination without proper grounds
Remove the patient from the practice immediately
Call the patient angrily
Alter the chart to make the visit look better
Tell staff to ignore all future calls
rationale: Complaints should be handled professionally. Retaliation, chart alteration, and abrupt abandonment increase risk and undermine trust.

text: An incapable patient has an old note saying only 'no heroic measures.' The family disagrees about tube feeding. What is best?
options: Clarify prior wishes and values with substitute decision-makers and use ethics or legal processes if disagreement persists
Treat the vague phrase as an automatic refusal of all care
Ignore the note completely
Let the loudest family member decide
Withdraw all treatment immediately
rationale: Advance directives must be interpreted in context. Vague language should prompt discussion about values, prior wishes, and best interests, not automatic withdrawal of all care.

text: An incapable patient has a clear, applicable written directive refusing ventilation if recovery is not possible. The family asks for ventilation anyway. What is best?
options: Follow the clear applicable prior capable wish while communicating compassionately with family
Ignore the directive because family is present
Ask the court in every case
Treat until the family changes its mind
Let the ICU bed status decide
rationale: A clear and applicable prior capable wish should guide care when the patient lacks capacity. Family support matters, but family preference does not erase the patient's prior wish.

text: A capable patient with advanced COPD asks to stop ventilatory support after understanding the likely outcome. Which statement is most accurate?
options: There is no ethical difference between withholding and withdrawing a treatment when consent rules are met
Withdrawal is always euthanasia
Family preference overrides the capable patient
Only a court can stop ventilatory support
The patient may refuse drugs but not machines
rationale: A capable patient may refuse or request withdrawal of treatment. Withholding and withdrawing are ethically similar when based on valid consent and appropriate care planning.

text: A dying patient with capacity has severe pain. Adequate opioid titration may carry a small risk of respiratory depression. What is the best approach?
options: Treat suffering proportionately with informed consent and careful monitoring
Withhold analgesia because any risk of shortened life is euthanasia
Use placebo only
Ask the family to decide despite capacity
Stop all opioids because the patient has a DNR
rationale: Relieving suffering is a core duty. Proportionate symptom treatment with consent is ethically acceptable even when it carries foreseeable risk, provided the intent is symptom relief and care is clinically appropriate.

text: A physician treated for substance use disorder wants to return to practice. What is the best principle?
options: Return may be possible with appropriate assessment, monitoring, support, and patient safety safeguards
A past disorder permanently prohibits all medical work
No monitoring is needed after treatment
Colleagues should hide any relapse affecting care
Only the physician decides readiness
rationale: Physician health concerns should be managed with compassion and patient safety. Return to practice may require physician health programs, regulatory conditions, monitoring, and workplace safeguards.

text: Police ask for the chart of a patient suspected of theft. The patient has not consented, and police provide no warrant or court order. What is the best response?
options: Release the chart because police requested it
Decline disclosure unless valid legal authority or a recognized exception applies
Destroy the chart
Give a verbal summary instead
Contact the patient’s employer
rationale: A police request alone does not usually authorize disclosure of personal health information. Consent, a warrant, a court order, or a specific legal exception is needed.

text: During an examination, a physician identifies findings that create reasonable grounds to suspect child abuse. What is the best next step?
options: Wait until abuse is proven
Confront the suspected person and conduct a full investigation
Promptly report to the designated child welfare authority as required by jurisdictional law
Ask the family to report themselves
Keep the information confidential in all circumstances
rationale: Canadian provinces and territories require reporting when there are reasonable grounds to suspect a child needs protection. Child welfare authorities investigate.

text: A patient has a medical condition that may make driving dangerous. What is the most appropriate physician action?
options: Use the same reporting rule in every province
Report only if the family requests it
Ignore the issue because driving is unrelated to healthcare
Assess and counsel the patient, document the discussion, and follow the applicable jurisdiction’s reporting law
Notify the patient’s employer
rationale: Fitness-to-drive reporting rules differ by province and territory. The clinician should assess risk, counsel the patient, document, and follow the applicable law.

text: A patient communicates a clear, serious, and imminent threat of bodily harm toward an identifiable person. What is the best confidentiality principle?
options: Consider lawful protective disclosure, limited to information necessary to address the risk
Never disclose without written consent
Publish the threat to the entire care team
Disclose the patient’s full lifetime record
Wait until harm occurs
rationale: A serious and imminent public-safety risk may justify disclosure without consent. Disclosure should be limited to what is necessary to protect the threatened person or others.

text: A patient asks to see their medical record. There is no identified risk to another person and no specific lawful exception. What is the best response?
options: Refuse because the physician owns the information
Release it only to a lawyer
Delete third-party notes without review
Provide only the billing sheet
Facilitate access according to applicable privacy law and record-access procedures
rationale: Patients generally have a right to access their health information, subject to limited legal exceptions and proper identity, scope, and redaction procedures.

text: A physician discovers that yesterday’s progress note contains an incorrect medication dose. What is the best documentation practice?
options: Erase the original entry
Add a dated, transparent correction or addendum that preserves the original record
Recreate the entire chart
Ask a colleague to alter the note
Leave the error unaddressed
rationale: Corrections should be transparent, dated, and traceable. The original record should not be concealed or overwritten.

text: A hospitalized patient is harmed by an unexpected medication administration error. After addressing immediate clinical needs, what should the responsible team do?
options: Avoid speaking until litigation is complete
State that a named nurse was negligent
Begin timely disclosure of known facts, express empathy, explain next steps, and document or report appropriately
Discuss only if the patient asks the exact cause
Alter the medication record
rationale: Disclosure of harm should be timely, factual, and compassionate. Early communication should include known facts, the current care plan, and appropriate follow-up.

text: During the first disclosure discussion after a patient safety incident, the cause remains uncertain. Which communication is best?
options: Assign blame to the most junior clinician
Guarantee there will be no consequences
State that negligence definitely occurred
Share known facts, avoid speculation or blame, and commit to follow-up as more becomes known
Withhold the patient’s current clinical status
rationale: Early disclosure should be factual. The team should avoid speculation or blame while analysis is incomplete and provide updates as more information becomes available.

text: Two clinically similar patients need one immediately available ICU bed. Which allocation approach is most ethically defensible?
options: Apply transparent, consistent, clinically relevant criteria through the established process
Prioritize the wealthier patient
Prioritize whoever has more social media followers
Let the treating physician choose secretly
Allocate based on perceived social worth
rationale: Scarce resources should be allocated using fair, transparent, consistently applied, clinically relevant criteria rather than social worth or personal preference.

text: A trainee believes a colleague’s proposed action creates an immediate, serious risk to a patient. What is the best response?
options: Remain silent to preserve collegiality
Post the concern publicly
Alter the colleague’s order without communication
Wait until after harm occurs
Address immediate safety, communicate respectfully, and escalate through appropriate clinical channels if unresolved
rationale: Patient safety comes first. Concerns should be raised promptly and professionally, with escalation through supervision or institutional pathways when needed.

text: A patient arrives with diabetes follow-up, knee pain, insomnia, and a work form. The appointment is short. What is the best opening response?
options: Ask what concerns matter most today, set a shared agenda, and arrange follow-up for items that cannot be addressed safely today
Tell the patient only one problem is allowed and end the visit
Complete the form first because it is fastest
Ignore the list and review only the diabetes labs
Refer the patient to emergency for all concerns
rationale: Good communication starts by identifying the patient agenda and negotiating priorities. It avoids missing the patient’s main concern and keeps the visit safe.

text: A 46-year-old presents with fatigue. Which opening question best supports patient-centred communication?
options: Can you tell me what has been happening and what worries you most?
Do you have depression, yes or no?
Why did you wait so long to come?
You are probably stressed, correct?
I will ask questions and you should answer only yes or no
rationale: Open questions allow the patient to describe symptoms, context, ideas, concerns, and expectations. Closed questions can follow after the story.

text: A patient with chest pain says, "I know it is probably nothing." What is the best next communication step while assessing risk?
options: Ask what they think is causing it, what worries them, and what they were hoping you could do today
Reassure immediately without asking more
Say chest pain is always anxiety in young patients
Tell them not to search online
Ask only about family history
rationale: ICE helps reveal hidden fear, expectations, and misunderstandings while clinical assessment continues. In chest pain, communication does not replace urgent risk assessment.

text: A patient begins crying after hearing that a biopsy is malignant. Which response is best?
options: I can see this is a lot to take in. I will sit with you, and we can go step by step.
At least we found it early, so do not cry
I have other patients waiting, so we need to move on
You need to be strong for your family
Everything happens for a reason
rationale: Empathy names emotion, respects silence, and offers support. False reassurance and minimizing distress harm trust.

text: A CT scan suggests metastatic cancer. The patient asks for the result. What is the best way to begin?
options: Check what they understand and want to know, give a warning shot, then share information in small clear pieces
